title: Customer Service & Family Support Certification
transcript: Welcome to the Customer Service and Family Support Certification.
In this course you will learn to give professional, compassionate and effective support to the families we serve.
Every interaction matters. How we communicate, listen and respond builds trust. You will learn how to:
Communicate professionally and confidently.
Practice active listening.
Show empathy.
Manage difficult conversations.
Handle healthcare calls with care.
Resolve concerns and document accurately.
In every module, you will practice and prove what you have learned.
Knowledge checks and games.
Real scenarios.
A mock call.
And a final exam.
Great customer service is not about having all the answers. It is about listening, communicating clearly, and building trust. Let us begin.

title: Our role and what families need
transcript: Customer Service Excellence. Our role and what families need.
For many families, we are their primary point of contact. The way we communicate can influence their trust in our organization.
Families generally expect four things.
Clarity. Explain information in simple, understandable language.
Responsiveness. Address concerns promptly, and say so when more time is needed.
Empathy. Recognize that families may be worried, frustrated, or uncertain.
Consistency. Give accurate information that follows approved procedures.
Put them together, and you get the positive experience formula.
Professionalism.
Plus empathy.
Plus resolution.
Equals trust.
Every interaction should help the family feel:
Heard.
Respected.
Supported.
Informed.
And valued.

title: Communicating professionally by phone
transcript: Customer Service Excellence. Communicating professionally by phone.
Tone and pace. Speak clearly, at a comfortable pace, in a calm, friendly, professional tone. Never sound rushed, bored, or impatient.
Listening. Let callers finish speaking. Don't talk over them, and ask questions when you need clarity.
Holds. Don't leave callers in silence. Ask permission before a hold, and return promptly with updates if the wait runs long.
Language. Avoid jargon and slang. Never argue, or match an angry tone. And don't promise what you can't confirm.
Instead of: Hold on.
Say: May I place you on a brief hold while I check that information for you?
And instead of staying silent,
say: Thank you for your patience. I'm reviewing the details now, and this may take a moment.

title: Active listening
transcript: Customer Service Excellence. Active listening.
Active listening means giving the caller your full attention, understanding their concern, and responding to what they actually said. It is how callers know they have been heard.
Five techniques will help.
Allow the caller to finish speaking.
Take notes on important details.
Repeat or summarize the main concern.
Ask clarifying questions.
And confirm that you understood correctly.
Here is what it sounds like.
Family member: I've called twice already, but I still haven't received an update.
Representative: I understand that you've contacted us twice and are still waiting for an update. Let me review the previous interactions so I can understand what's happened. Is that correct?
It works because callers feel supported when they know we have listened and understood their concerns.

title: Demonstrating empathy
transcript: Customer Service Excellence. Demonstrating empathy.
Next, empathy. Empathy means recognizing and acknowledging another person's feelings or concerns.
These statements can help families feel heard.
Representative: I understand why you're concerned.
Representative: I can see how this situation has been frustrating.
Representative: Thank you for bringing this to our attention.
Representative: I'm sorry you've had to follow up more than once.
Representative: Let's review what happened and see what we can do next.
Finally, a quick self-check. After every call, ask yourself:
Did I listen carefully?
Did I communicate clearly?
Did I provide accurate information?
Does the caller understand the next steps?

title: The LEARN framework
transcript: Customer Service Excellence. The LEARN framework.
Use the LEARN framework on every call.
L, Listen. Allow the caller to explain the concern without unnecessary interruptions.
E, Empathize. Acknowledge the caller's feelings or experience.
A, Assess. Ask questions, review the available information, and identify the issue.
R, Resolve. Offer an appropriate solution, or take the next action within your authority.
N, Next steps. Explain what happens next, who is responsible, and when to expect an update, if the timeline is confirmed.
Here it is in action, when a family member has not received a promised update.
Listen: hear the full concern.
Empathize: acknowledge the frustration.
Assess: review previous notes and the current status.
Resolve: provide an answer, or contact the appropriate team.
Next steps: explain the follow-up plan, and document the commitment.

title: Asking the right questions
transcript: Customer Service Excellence. Asking the right questions.
Good questions help us understand the situation, avoid assumptions, and identify the correct next step.
Helpful questions sound like this.
Can you tell me more about what happened?
When did you first notice the issue?
Have you received any updates so far?
Can you confirm which request you're referring to?
What outcome are you hoping for?
But avoid accusatory questions.
Instead of: Why didn't you follow the instructions?
Say: Can you walk me through what happened when you followed the instructions?
And instead of: Why are you calling again?
Say: I understand you've contacted us before. Let me review the previous notes so we can determine the next step.

title: Managing expectations
transcript: Customer Service Excellence. Managing expectations.
Uncertainty can increase frustration, especially when families are waiting for important information.
Always explain:
What is known about the situation.
What action will be taken.
Who is responsible for the next step.
When an update is expected, if confirmed.
And what the caller should do if they do not receive the update.
A weak response: We'll get back to you.
A better one: Our team is reviewing your request. You can expect an update by tomorrow afternoon. Use this wording only when the timeline is confirmed and you are authorized to share it.
When the timeline is not confirmed, say so.
Representative: I'll check with the appropriate team to confirm the expected timeline. I'll explain the follow-up process once I have that information.

title: Handling difficult conversations
transcript: Customer Service Excellence. Handling difficult conversations.
Upset or frustrated.
Confused about a process.
Impatient about delays.
Disappointed with a previous response.
Or concerned because they have contacted us several times.
Avoid arguing or becoming defensive.
Matching their volume or tone.
Or making promises just to end the conversation.
Instead, speak calmly and clearly.
Acknowledge their frustration.
Offer realistic options.
And explain the next steps.
Family member: This is ridiculous! I've called three times and nobody has helped me!
Representative: I'm sorry you've had to contact us multiple times without getting the resolution you need. Let me review the previous notes and see what we can do next.
Do not take frustration personally. Focus on the issue, not the caller's tone. If a caller becomes threatening or abusive, follow the organization's safety and call-termination policy.

title: Unknown answers and escalation
transcript: Customer Service Excellence. Unknown answers and escalation.
When you don't know the answer, never guess. Incorrect information damages trust and creates more problems.
Instead:
Acknowledge the question.
Check approved resources.
Consult the appropriate team or a supervisor if needed.
Explain what you can confirm.
Give a follow-up plan.
And document the action required.
Escalate according to policy when:
The issue is outside your authority.
It can't be resolved through normal procedures.
A supervisor is requested.
A policy exception is requested.
A complaint involves a sensitive or serious concern.
Or there are potential legal, privacy, or safety issues.

Before escalating, prepare a brief summary, relevant dates, actions already taken, outstanding commitments, and the outcome the caller wants. If a supervisor is requested, follow the escalation procedure.

title: Documentation standards
transcript: Customer Service Excellence. Documentation standards.
Accurate documentation helps team members understand what happened, continue the work, and follow through on commitments.
A call record includes, as applicable:
The date and time of the call.
The main concern, and account details as policy allows.
Key facts, and the information you reviewed.
Actions taken.
Information communicated.
And the resolution, or the follow-up owner and timeline, if confirmed.
Use objective, factual language.
Record commitments accurately.
Follow approved retention policies.
Avoid personal opinions or emotional judgments.
And leave out unnecessary sensitive information.

Here is an example note. Family member called requesting an update on a pending request. Confirmed that the request remains under review, and advised that the follow-up timeline would be confirmed with the responsible team. Follow-up required.

title: The seven steps of a call, and key takeaways
transcript: Customer Service Excellence. The seven steps of a call, and key takeaways.
Every professional call follows seven steps.
One, greeting. Introduce yourself.
Two, verification. Complete the required checks before sharing any private information.
Three, listening. Understand the concern.
Four, investigation. Review and identify the action.
Five, resolve or escalate.
Six, next steps. Explain follow-up and confirmed timelines.
Seven, closing. Summarize and close courteously.
Great service is not about having every answer. It is about:
Listening carefully.
Showing empathy.
Protecting confidential information.
Setting realistic expectations.
Escalating appropriately.
And documenting and following through.
Every call is an opportunity to build trust, with professionalism, respect, and care.

title: Professional communication
transcript: Professional communication.
Callers often judge service by how it was communicated, not only by the result. Aim to be understood, be respectful, and leave the person knowing what happens next.
Five habits make a voice easy to trust.
Speak clearly.
Speak confidently.
Stay calm.
Do not interrupt.
And use simple words.
Instead of: I don't know.
Say: Let me verify that for you.
Instead of: That's not my department.
Say: I will find the right person for that.
Every email and chat message has five parts, in this order.
A greeting, using their name.
The purpose, in one sentence.
The information.
The next step.
And a polite closing.
Whenever you finish a conversation, explain three things.
The timeline.
Who is responsible.
And the follow-up plan.
With callers in the United States, lead with the answer, and be warm and direct. Clarity matters more than accent. If you are unsure, check and restate.

title: Confidentiality and boundaries
transcript: Confidentiality and boundaries.
Families trust us with private information. Knowing when to say, I cannot share that, is as important as knowing what to say.
Before you discuss any details, confirm who the person is, and that they may have the information.
Ask who they are.
Check the record.
Only then share what they may have.

I am his sister. I am calling for my neighbour. These sound reasonable, and they are the most common way private information is shared by mistake. A friendly voice or a good reason does not replace the check.
Confidentiality is also about where and how you work.
Take calls where nobody else can overhear.
No detailed messages on shared voicemail.
No talking about callers on social media.
And close the case when you step away.
We help with process.
We do not give medical advice.
Legal advice.
Or financial advice, even when someone seems to need it.
If you make a mistake, tell your lead and report it straight away. Fast reporting limits harm. Reporting is never punished.

title: Healthcare support calls
transcript: Healthcare support calls.
Many of our calls come from patients, their relatives, and caregivers or family of people living in a care home. They need to be heard first and helped second.
We are not clinicians. We listen, verify, route and document.
We listen and take the request.
Verify who is calling.
Route it with a time frame.
And write a clear note.
We never say what a symptom or result means.
Say it is probably fine.
Suggest a dose or medicine.
Or promise an approval.
Appointments: verify first.
Refills and records: route with a time frame.
Results worry: listen, do not interpret, arrange a call from the care team.
Billing: do not guess coverage.
A possible emergency: follow the client's emergency steps.
If a call sounds like an emergency, do not judge how serious it is. Act.
Stay calm and listen.
Tell them to call emergency services.
Follow the client's steps, and alert your lead.
And record the time, the words and what you said.
A routine request does not come first when a person's safety may be at risk. Never book, never wait, never reassure. Each client's own steps are taught in that client's add-on module.

title: Difficult callers
transcript: Difficult callers.
Callers are not difficult people. They are people having a difficult time. What you hear usually points to something they need.
Shouting: to be heard, then a plan.
The same question again: reassurance and a next step.
Confusion: slower, simpler steps.
Demands: respect and a clear option.
Calling again and again: a problem never solved.
Angry: let them vent briefly, then steer to solving.
Anxious: answer calmly, with a next step and a time.
Confused: one step at a time, checking understanding.
Demanding: stay professional, and offer escalation.
Callers who ring again and again usually have a problem that was never solved. Ask what is still open, then close the loop with a clear owner and time.
You do not have to accept being abused. If a caller uses threats or slurs:
Give one calm warning.
If it continues, end the call, following your client's policy.
And tell your lead.
After a hard call, write down the facts, not opinions, and take a short reset before the next call.

title: Worked example: a routine request
transcript: Worked example. A routine request.
In this call, a family member wants to update their own contact details.
Representative: Thank you for calling. My name is Ana. How may I help you today?
Family member: Hi. I would like to change the phone number you have on my file.
Representative: I'm happy to help with that. First I need to verify who I'm speaking with. May I have your full name and your reference, please?
Family member: Of course. It's Carla Reyes, and the reference is in my last email.
Representative: Thank you, Carla. That matches our record. What is the new number?
Family member: It's my new mobile. I'll read it out.
Representative: Thank you. Let me read it back to make sure it's correct. I've updated your file and added a note about the change. Is there anything else I can help with?
What worked in this call:
A professional greeting.
Verified who she was before changing anything.
Read the new detail back to confirm it.
Added a note about the change.
And offered further help.

title: Worked example: a form returned twice
transcript: Worked example. A form returned twice.
In this call, a family member is frustrated that a form they sent has come back twice.
Family member: I have sent this form twice and it keeps coming back to me!
Representative: I'm sorry that has happened twice. Let me make sure I understand. You sent the form, and it was returned each time. Is that right?
Family member: Yes, and nobody tells me what is missing.
Representative: That would frustrate anyone. Let me check the notes on your file, so you don't have to explain it all again.
Family member: Fine. What happens after that?

Representative: Once I confirm what is missing, I'll explain how to send it and what to expect. I'll also note on your file that you've already sent it twice, so the next person doesn't ask you to start over. I can't promise a processing time until it's confirmed.
What worked in this call:
Apologized and acknowledged the frustration.
Checked that she understood the problem correctly.
Reviewed the notes, so the caller did not repeat everything.
Explained the next step.
And made no promise about a time that was not confirmed.

title: Worked example: a request for a supervisor
transcript: Worked example. A request for a supervisor.
In this call, a family member asks to speak with a supervisor.
Family member: I would like to speak with a supervisor.
Representative: Of course. I'll help you with that. If you're comfortable, could you tell me briefly what it's about, so I can pass it along?
Family member: I missed a deadline by one day, and I was told no exception is possible.

Representative: Thank you for explaining. I understand you would like someone to review that. I'll follow our process to connect you with a supervisor, and I'll share your summary so you don't have to repeat it.
Family member: How long will that take?
Representative: I'll check how the process works and tell you the next step. I don't want to give you a wait time that I can't confirm.
What worked in this call:
Honored the request without arguing.
Asked permission before gathering details.
Passed the summary on, so the caller did not repeat it.
Followed the escalation process.
And did not invent a wait time.
